sets.relationshipLabel: thing and the feature it always has
sets.explanation: A piton always has an eye and a carabiner always has a gate — each object named alongside the part that defines its function.

sets.relationshipLabel: category of peak and a named member of it
sets.explanation: Eight-thousander and fourteener are altitude categories, with K2 and Rainier standing as their real-world examples.

sets.relationshipLabel: worker and the tool of their trade
sets.explanation: A belayer is defined by their belay device just as a lead climber is defined by the rack they carry.

sets.relationshipLabel: opening stage of the larger whole it belongs to
sets.explanation: The approach opens a route and the basecamp opens an expedition — each is the first phase of something bigger, not a separate thing.

glossary.definition: A mountain whose summit rises above 8,000 meters, a rare height only a handful of peaks on Earth reach.

definitions.definition: A metal spike hammered into cracks in rock to anchor a rope.
The little hole in a piece of hardware where you clip a rope or carabiner.
A metal loop with a spring-loaded clip, used to connect ropes and gear quickly and safely.
The hinged part of a clip that swings open so you can hook things onto it.
A mountain whose summit rises above 8,000 meters, a rare height only a handful of peaks on Earth reach.
A brutally steep, icy peak in the Karakoram, famous as one of the deadliest mountains to climb.
A mountain that tops 14,000 feet, a popular benchmark height for hikers and climbers in the US.
A massive glacier-covered volcano in Washington State, a classic goal for mountaineers.
The person managing the rope to catch a climber safely if they fall.
A small metal gadget that lets a rope feed smoothly while adding friction to stop a fall.
The climber who goes up first, placing protection and clipping the rope as they go.
The collection of gear a climber carries to place protection along a climb.
The hike or trek you do just to reach the base of the actual climb.
The specific path up a cliff or mountain that climbers follow to the top.
The staging area at the bottom of a mountain where climbers gather supplies before heading up.
A long, organized journey to climb a big mountain, often taking weeks and lots of planning.
